title: TCP: Fix conversation overlapping when reusing ports
description:
Identification of the appropriate conversation is randomly
wrong when both TCP ports are reused.
Mark the real last conversation packet in packet list.
Compliance with the documentation which states that
conversations are not sensitive to the packet direction.
Closes #15097.

notes.body:
2 changes here to solve the issue :
- find_conversation_pinfo() is no more updating the conversation frame queue (was this the right place anyway ?), the queue is instead updated in packet-tcp. Moreover trying to restore the old value in packet-tcp is removed, it wasn't working well as the value was updated too early as said just above. Some gains on packet-tcp readability.
- find_conversation_pinfo() is now looking for another potential conversation on the other direction, instead of trying to do this in packet-tcp. This is more in conformity with the documentation (_"A conversation is not sensitive to the direction of the packet"_).

As expected unluckily, this breaks some other calls to find_conversation_pinfo() in other dissectors. The solution to this new behavior : either move my change to a new dedicated find_conversation_pinfo() for packet-tcp and we're done, or extend my work in the other concerned dissectors to fix these regressions. Let's talk and let me know how do you see things here.

On the first change:

Possibly call `find_conversation_pinfo()` in packet-tcp, but instead call `find_conversation` (which doesn't update the last_frame) the way it was done in `packet-tcp` before 23afd9a18453c23cfbbc6a63f52b2e6e64e0056c.

As you note, the code [intended to save and reset the last frame in packet-tcp](epan/dissectors/packet-tcp.c#L6551-6553) doesn't work currently since `find_conversation_pinfo` sets the last frame.

Unfortunately, even reverting that part there doesn't necessarily help in most cases. A lot of subdissectors still call `find_or_create_conversation` (which calls `find_conversation_pinfo`, and TCP itself calls `find_or_create_conversation` when `get_tcp_conversation_data` is called without the conversation, which happens a lot in the TCP dissector when dissecting certain options, etc. So those subdissectors will still end up finding the first conversation and updating the `last_frame`.

On the second change:

Note that `find_conversation` (and thus `find_conversation_pinfo`) already searches for conversations in both directions, as you've found it just takes any conversation in the same direction before a more recent conversation in the other direction. As you note, that breaks the idea of conversations not being sensitive to direction.

On the other hand, there are dissectors that want the current behavior because they really do want one-way conversations where direction matters. Some of those dissectors go through some ugly hacks after getting a conversation in order to figure out which direction it is.  Arguably the _right way_ for some of those dissectors is to use the endpoint API, but then there's the issue that some of them do not have their own addressing scheme (or their addresses aren't unique across multiple conversations, so they'd need a multilayered solution), like MP2T.

Perhaps the answer is to add a new option / flag for `find_conversation` and `find_conversation_pinfo` (and extend `find_or_create_conversation` to take options) that controls the behavior. I think in reality that most dissectors would want one of two behaviors:

1. Most recent convo in created in either direction
2. Most recent convo in created in same direction

Neither of which is the current behavior of
Most recent convo created in same direction; if no dissector created in same direction, most recent in opposite direction.

Thanks @johnthacker for the time spent here and the quality of the feedback I was requesting/expecting.

I pushed another implementation which is more compliant to the original idea (extending the conversation in `find_conversation_pinfo`) while still changing the conversation identification part in `packet-tcp`.

New helper functions are introduced (`find_conversation_oriented `, `find_conversation_pinfo_oriented `, `find_or_create_conversation_oriented`) then one who knows what behavior to expect will not be misdirected by the current behavior (most recent in same direction, if none then most recent in opposite direction).

When calling the old helper functions, this will find orientation-agnostic conversations as expected in the documentation.

The current identification algo (most recent in same direction, if none then most recent in opposite direction) is changed for a more deterministic one (if conversation is oriented return what is found or nothing, or return the more recent match).

I don't have any pcap of an oriented protocol to check how it behaves, if you have any idea of what test to perform please let me know.

changed the description

The patch looks for fully matching conversations in both directions and then takes the most recent, instead of preferring the most recent conversation in the same direction to any conversation in the other direction.

This changes the way conversations work, so it's more than just a TCP change. I believe that most dissectors that really want a one way conversation (e.g. RTP) end up creating a wildcarded conversation with no address B and never fill it in, so it may not break things. As you note, you are making the behavior match the comments and documentation.

This patch does not make the analogous changes for searching for wildcarded conversations. The rest of `find_conversation` is still preferring matches in the original direction (for example, anything with the same address A and wildcarded address B is preferred over same B and wildcarded A.) We might eventually want to change that too.

At least recently, the save last frame part never worked, because `find_conversation_pinfo` was updating it before it was ever saved. (Possibly previously it did not do this.) With these changes, by calling `find_conversation` instead, it seems like `last_frame` is never updated for TCP. Perhaps it should be (or perhaps not, what is it used for currently?)

> The patch looks for fully matching conversations in both directions and then takes the most recent

It is direction agnostic, or ignorant.

> This changes the way conversations work, so it's more than just a TCP change.

Exactly. I first wrote other methods calling the methods that we already have, but that meant adding these new methods in the API (more things to document, possibly giving new practices to new dissector writers). Not 100% sure what is the best choice according to wireshark's standards (correcting the software where necessary to be compliant with the well-understood documentation, or increase the API and give new coding rules).

> it seems like `last_frame` is never updated for TCP.

I will check. All other protocols need to be checked also.

> It is direction agnostic, or ignorant.

For fully matching conversations. It doesn't change the behavior when looking for conversations that only match on one address or port, including as a fallback for when there are no fully matching conversations but it has all information. In those cases, it still searches one direction, then the other, and prefers an earlier conversation from one direction to a later one in the opposite direction. (That doesn't affect TCP though.)

What this doesn't solve (and is far more tricky) is a case where the conversations actually _do_ overlap because the TCP packets arrived out of order. We could detect that with a lot of work in certain cases and correctly retrieve the earlier conversation, but all the calls to `find_conversation_pinfo()` scattered in other places would still find the earlier conversation, so that's an issue for other work.

Can you add a line to as mentioned above in the TCP dissector to ensure that `conv->last_frame` gets set there (instead of depending on it luckily getting set elsewhere in the dissector when `find_conversation_pinfo()` or `find_or_create_conversation()` is called?) If you do that, I think it's ready.

I added back `conv->last_frame` (which was here in my first version but after testing and testing more I saw that finally things were working without, and forgot to add it again). Anyway, it's justified to keep it, and it moves early that list tail.

> ..is a case where the conversations actually *do* overlap because the TCP packets arrived out of order.

The weapons used by TCP and clients to avoid this situation are the TIME_WAIT state, the random Initial Sequence Number, and the random client port. In practice such case could maybe happen, particularly when trying to provoke it (with a curl loop reusing the client port associated to any hardware known for randomly duplicating packets), but I have no material showing how this behaves. I'll try again to generate such capture. Finally I would then expect _Previous Segment Not Seen/Packet Out-of-Order_ warning messages.
Despite all that I wrote, I think this is generally correct, I will just test it on a few protocols when I have a chance to see if anything depends on the undocumented behavior.
For example MySQL uses conversations, although it's not in the conversations pop-up window.
Thanks for the approval and congrats for your upgrade to the approval team, that's not nothing.
